subject: Communication
title: The Steeple: The Confidence Gesture
description: A quick win: understand The Steeple: The Confidence Gesture.

hook.text: A lawyer touches her fingertips together in a steeple shape. Before she speaks, you already know she's confident.

buildup.text: The steeple — fingertips pressed together — is one of the most reliable indicators of confidence and authority.

discovery.text: Joe Navarro, former FBI agent, calls it a 'high-confidence display' seen in leaders and experts worldwide.

twist.text: When confidence drops, the steeple collapses into interlocked fingers or hand-wringing — the reverse signal.

climax.text: Angela Merkel's signature steeple became an icon of composed leadership — dubbed the 'Merkel-Raute.'

punchline.text: Fingertips together: confidence. Fingers interlocked: doubt.

quiz.question: What does the hand steeple gesture typically signal?

details.summary: Steepling—pressing the fingertips of both hands together—is one of the most reliable indicators of confidence and authority. Leaders and experts use it naturally when they feel certain about what they are saying.
details.whyItMatters: Recognizing steepling helps read confidence levels in meetings, negotiations, and presentations, providing insight into someone's certainty.
takeaways: It appears most often during moments of certainty
Lowering the steeple may indicate doubt or reconsideration

faq.question: Can you use steepling to appear more confident?
faq.answer: Yes. Deliberately steepling during a presentation or negotiation can project authority. However, it works best when paired with genuinely confident speech. Steepling while sounding uncertain creates a mismatch that undermines credibility.

faq.question: What does a lowered steeple indicate?
faq.answer: When someone drops from a raised steeple to a lowered position or interlaces their fingers, it often signals a shift from confidence to uncertainty or a willingness to listen rather than assert.
